initial_requirements: The Southwest Florida Water Management District needs a GIS-based Water Use Tracking System for District employees and external customers. The system should support spatial and temporal analysis of regulatory and resource-management data, particularly permitted and actual water use. It is intended to replace inconsistent manual and semi-automated analyses and help staff evaluate water-use trends and assess the effects of management rules.

messages.content: What are the primary goals and success criteria for the Water Use Tracking System, and which outcomes matter most to District employees and external customers?

The main goal is to give staff and customers a reliable, GIS-based way to analyze permitted and actual water use without all the manual work we do now. Success means people can quickly find accurate spatial and temporal data, compare trends over time, and use the same system instead of separate spreadsheets and ad hoc tools. For District employees, the most important outcome is better regulatory and resource-management decisions with less time spent assembling data. For external customers, it’s easier access to their water-use information and clearer, more consistent reporting.

What levels of spatial and temporal detail should the system support for water-use analysis and reporting—for example, specific geographic units, map layers, and time intervals such as daily, monthly, annual, or permit-term views?

We definitely need enough spatial detail to work at the parcel and permit level, and to view things by well, facility, basin, and other District geographic areas as needed. The map layers should let staff overlay permitted use, actual use, water resources, and management boundaries so they can see relationships clearly. On the time side, monthly and annual views are the most important for routine analysis and reporting, but we also need permit-term and multi-year trend views. I’m not sure daily analysis is a core need for everyone, though it might be useful in some cases if the data supports it.

In the cases where daily water-use analysis would be useful, what specific user tasks or investigations should the system support, and how would those daily views differ from the routine monthly, annual, or permit-term analyses?

Daily views would mainly be for exception checking and short-term investigations, like looking into unusual pump activity, verifying a reported spike, or checking whether a specific condition or restriction was met on a given day. Those views would be more about pinpointing events and anomalies than doing standard compliance or trend reporting. The monthly, annual, and permit-term views are the routine ones for summarizing use, comparing against permitted amounts, and spotting longer-term patterns. Daily analysis would need finer granularity and probably more detail in the display, while the longer views can focus more on totals and trends.

What different access levels or permissions should the system provide for District employees versus external customers, and what should external customers be able to view, analyze, or do on their own without staff assistance?

District employees need broader access because they’ll be doing the regulatory and management work, so they should be able to see internal analysis tools, cross-permit comparisons, mapping layers, and data that may not be exposed externally. External customers should have access to their own permit and water-use information, along with basic maps, summaries, and reports that help them understand their usage. They should be able to view and analyze their own data on their own, but not see other customers’ information or perform staff-only administrative functions. Anything beyond that, like changing official records or running internal regulatory reviews, would stay with District staff.

Which source systems or datasets will the Water Use Tracking System need to integrate with, and what should be included in that integration—such as permitted-use records, actual-use submissions, GIS layers, permit metadata, water-resource boundaries, or other external/internal data sources?

At a minimum, it needs to pull in the permit records, the permitted-use allocations, and the actual-use submissions, because those are the core of the tracking and comparison work. It also needs the GIS layers that staff use for parcels, wells, facilities, and District boundaries or management areas, plus permit metadata so the records can be tied back to the right customer and location. We’d likely also want water-resource boundary data and maybe supporting reference layers, but I’d need to verify whether those come from internal systems or external sources. The main thing is that the system should keep the permit and usage data synchronized enough that staff aren’t reconciling everything manually.

To support reliable reporting without manual reconciliation, what are the required data freshness and synchronization rules for permit and usage data—for example, which system should be treated as the source of truth, how conflicts or mismatches should be resolved, and how quickly updates need to propagate after new submissions or corrections?

The source of truth should be the District’s official permit and reporting systems, not the tracking application itself. This system should mirror those authoritative records and flag mismatches instead of trying to overwrite them on its own. New submissions and corrections should propagate quickly enough that staff are working with current information, ideally within the same business day if possible, but I don’t have a firm service-level target yet. If there’s a conflict, the system should preserve the official record, show the discrepancy, and let staff resolve it through the normal review process.

When the system mirrors official permit and usage records, what provenance details should it capture and display for each record or change event—for example, source system, submission date/time, who submitted or approved it, version history, and any notes needed to explain how the data became authoritative?

It should definitely capture the source system, the submission or update timestamp, and whichever user or office made the change if that information is available from the authoritative system. Version history is important too, so staff can see what changed and when, especially if a permit or usage report was corrected after the fact. If there are approval steps or review notes in the official process, those should be carried through as well because they explain why a record is authoritative. We’d also want audit notes or comments for exceptions, but the exact fields may depend on what the source systems can provide.
